head: Term
Meaning
Where it comes from
rows: Benchmark price

The board’s modelled price of a typical home of a given type and area, built from home features rather than from the prices of the homes that happened to sell. It is not an average or a median of sales.
MLS® Home Price Index, GVR and FVREB
Index
The benchmark expressed against January 2005 = 100, so you can compare long-term growth between areas.
MLS® Home Price Index
Listed (inventory)
Homes listed for sale at the end of the month.
SnapStats; board statistics call this active listings
Sold (sales)
Homes that sold during the month.
SnapStats; board statistics
Sales ratio

Homes sold in the month divided by homes listed, as a percentage. On the reports’ own scale under 12% is a buyers’ market, 12% to 20% is balanced and over 20% is a sellers’ market. With fewer than ten homes listed, one sale moves the ratio a long way, so it is a rough signal.
SnapStats
Reported sale price
The one sale-price figure the reports give each month. The reports do not say whether it is an average or a median, so it shows direction and is not a valuation of any one home.
SnapStats
Days on market
SnapStats
Sale-to-list price ratio
The sale price as a percentage of the last list price.
SnapStats
Median and average price
The middle sale price and the arithmetic mean of sale prices in the month, as the board publishes them.
FVREB statistics
Median (sold figures)
The middle value of the sales in the group: half sold for more and half for less. It is not an average, so one very high or very low sale does not move it.
Paragon closed sales
Sold vs list
The sale price as a percentage of the last list price, as a median across the sales in the group. “Sold above list” is the share that sold for more than the last list price.
Paragon closed sales
Median per square foot
Sale price divided by the floor area in the listing, as a median. Floor areas are as entered by the listing agent.
Paragon closed sales
Condos and townhomes combined

The SnapStats monthly reports give condos and townhomes as one line, so the month-by-month tables cover both. The “what sold” tables from the MLS® closed sales do separate them, and the boards’ own apartment and townhouse benchmarks are used where available.

blocks.text: We only say a price or a count rose or fell when the data can carry it. Two rules apply everywhere on the site, and they are applied by the same code each month:

items.t: A change of less than 1.5% is called "little changed", with the figure shown, and is never described as a rise or fall.

A change in the number of listings or sales is not described as a trend when either count is under 3. One listing more or less is noise, and the page gives the two counts and says they are too few to call a rise or fall.

blocks.text: Percent changes in the Home Price Index are shown as the board publishes them (1 month, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, 3 years, 5 years, 10 years). Counts of listings and sales are compared from the first month we hold (June 2026) to the latest month, and the month is named in the sentence.

The same thinness rule applies to sold figures. A median is published only where at least 5 homes sold in the group, a count is mentioned only where at least 3 sold, and a building or complex is named with a price only with at least 5 sales. A quarter-by-quarter table appears only when each of the four quarters has at least 5 sales, and it is shown as figures, not described as a trend.
Months, refreshes and what is not published

items.t: Each table and each figure in a sentence names its month. A page is only as current as the month it names.
Figures are refreshed when a month’s reports are released. Market answers that carry a date become out of date the following month until they are refreshed.
We do not publish the sale price or address of an individual home from the MLS® system, and every figure we add comes from a source named on this page.

blocks.text: What this data cannot tell you

Averages and benchmarks describe a market, not your home. A price index cannot see the condition of a house, its lot, a view, a suite or a building’s strata finances, and community figures can rest on very few sales. For a number you can use in a decision about a specific address, ask Jared for a comparable-sales review.

The data relating to real estate on this website comes in part from the MLS® Reciprocity program of Greater Vancouver REALTORS® (GVR), the Fraser Valley Real Estate Board (FVREB) or the Chilliwack and District Real Estate Board (CADREB). The boards assume no responsibility for its accuracy.
Notes that apply to every table
Each table on this site names its source in one line and links here. These are the definitions and limits behind those lines.

items.t: Sales come from Paragon, the MLS® system Jared’s office uses. Where a table counts pending sales, a pending sale is firm but has not completed, so its price can still change; sales that fell through are left out. Where a source line says closed sales, pending sales are not counted.

Median means the middle price: half sold for more and half for less. An average is the total of sale prices divided by the number of sales, so it moves with the mix of homes that sold. A monthly median or average from fewer than 3 sales is not read as a trend.
A median, row, community, building, price band or quarter is shown only where at least 5 homes sold; with fewer, one sale would be the whole figure. A dash means fewer than 5.

Lists of a niche type (legal suites, penthouses, golf course homes) name a neighbourhood at 3 or more sales and show its median at 5 or more. School tables leave out schools with fewer than 10 sales nearby.
Duplexes and row houses count in "All homes" only. A quarter is shown only when each of the four has 5 or more sales, and the change is not called a trend.
Sold vs list is the sale price as a percentage of the last list price.

A legal suite means Paragon lists the suite as Legal Suite or Licensed Suite; an unauthorized suite is one the listing marks Unauthorized Suite; houses with no suite, or with the field left blank, are in neither column.

A penthouse is a condo whose Paragon style field includes Penthouse. A golf course home is a detached house whose Site Influences field lists Golf Course Nearby or Golf Course Dev.; the listing agent chooses the flag, so treat counts as a floor.
Building names are as entered in the MLS® listings; a building’s price is the median of its sales, not any one home.

The benchmark (MLS® Home Price Index) is the board’s modelled price for a typical home of a type and area, not an average or median of sales. The index sets January 2005 at 100. Changes are as published; the text calls a change a rise or fall only at 1.5% or more.

Monthly listing and sales counts are MLS® data from the Greater Vancouver REALTORS® and the Fraser Valley Real Estate Board, compiled by SnapStats®. Sales ratio is homes sold divided by homes listed in the month; on the reports’ own scale under 12% is a buyers’ market, 12% to 20% balanced and over 20% a sellers’ market. With fewer than ten homes listed, one sale moves the ratio a long way, and ranks count only communities with at least ten listed.

Shares are a community’s count divided by its city’s total for the same month and home type. The reports count condos and townhomes together in one line, and give one sale-price figure a month without saying whether it is an average or a median, so use it for direction, not as a valuation.

Falling listings with steady sales mean homes are being absorbed faster; rising listings with steady sales mean more choice for buyers. A sellers’ best bet is a community where homes sell quickly against the number listed; a buyers’ best bet is the reverse.
Price-range tables show the five ranges with the most listings and leave out ranges with nothing listed and nothing sold. Period totals add up the sales in every neighbourhood.
Distances to schools are straight-line from the school coordinates, not walking or driving routes.

faq.q: Where does the data on jaredgibbons.ca come from?
faq.a: From the monthly SnapStats® community reports, the Greater Vancouver REALTORS® and Fraser Valley Real Estate Board statistics and MLS® Home Price Index packages, and the BC Data Catalogue for schools and child care. Each table names its source and month.
The board’s modelled price for a typical home of a given type and area. It is not the average or median of homes that sold, so it moves more smoothly and is not a valuation of any one home.

faq.q: What is the sales ratio and what do 12% and 20% mean?
faq.a: It is homes sold in the month divided by homes listed. On the reports’ own scale, under 12% is a buyers’ market, 12% to 20% is balanced and over 20% is a sellers’ market. Below ten listings, one sale moves it a long way.

faq.q: When does the site call a price or count a rise or a fall?
faq.a: Only when the change is 1.5% or more, and for counts only when both months have at least 3 listings or sales. Smaller changes are described as little changed and thin counts are not described as a trend.

faq.q: How often is the data updated?
faq.a: When each month’s reports are released. Every figure names its month, so you can see how current it is.

faq.q: Why do some tables cover condos and townhomes together?
faq.a: The SnapStats monthly reports give them as one line. The sold-price tables come from MLS® closed sales and show condos and townhomes separately, and the boards’ apartment and townhouse benchmarks are used where they are available.

faq.q: Do you publish sold prices for individual homes?
faq.a: No. The site shows grouped figures such as the median price of the sales in a community or building, and does not show the sale price or address of an individual MLS® sale.
